Adding the advisory IDs and a per-branch check. All three advisories are fixed in undici [7.30.1](https://www.npmjs.com/package/undici/v/7.30.1):

- [GHSA-xjj6-f33q-929c](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xjj6-f33q-929c) / CVE-2026-109869 (high, CVSS 7.5): Denial of Service via unhandled error on excessive content-encodings, affects `>= 7.18.0, < 7.30.1`
- [GHSA-4qv8-2p9j-2685](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4qv8-2p9j-2685) / CVE-2026-109924 (moderate, CVSS 5.9): Denial of Service via unbounded memory in the EventSource parser, affects `>= 7.0.0, < 7.30.1`
- [GHSA-f72v-6w45-q472](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f72v-6w45-q472) / CVE-2026-109841 (moderate, CVSS 5.9): Subresource Integrity bypass via non-lowercase algorithm tokens, affects `>= 7.15.0, < 7.30.1`

Affected lines, confirming the assessment above:

- **21.2.x** (21.2.28, latest `v21-lts`): `@angular/build` has `"undici": "7.29.1"` in its `dependencies`, so every v21 install gets the vulnerable version.
- **20.3.x** (20.3.41): no published package depends on undici. A fresh install only gets undici 6.29.1 via `node-gyp` (`^6.25.0`), which is already patched, and `npm audit` reports 0 vulnerabilities. The repo still pins 7.29.1 as a devDependency (root and `@angular-devkit/build-angular`).
- **22.2.x** (22.2.4): no published package depends on undici. The repo devDependency is 8.10.2 (the 8.x fix is 8.12.2). The Dependency Dashboard (#23493) already has "update dependency undici to v8.12.3 (22.2.x)" waiting for approval.

`npm install @angular/build@21` followed by `npm audit`:

```text
# npm audit report

undici  7.0.0 - 7.30.0
Severity: high
undici vulnerable to Denial of Service via unbounded memory in the EventSource parser - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4qv8-2p9j-2685
undici vulnerable to Subresource Integrity bypass via non-lowercase algorithm tokens - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f72v-6w45-q472
undici vulnerable to Denial of Service via unhandled error on excessive content-encodings - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xjj6-f33q-929c
fix available via `npm audit fix --force`
Will install @angular/build@22.2.4, which is a breaking change
node_modules/undici
  @angular/build  21.0.0-next.0 - 21.2.28
  Depends on vulnerable versions of undici
  node_modules/@angular/build

2 vulnerabilities (1 moderate, 1 high)

To address all issues (including breaking changes), run:
  npm audit fix --force
```

Fix PRs, in the same shape as the previous undici backports (#34053, #34052):

- 21.2.x: #34521
- 20.3.x: #34522 (devDependency only)

Hi @cracksalad,

To answer your questions:

1. **Pinning versions:** We deliberately pin dependencies in the CLI to guarantee deterministic builds and prevent unexpected regressions. With build tooling and compilers (such as Vite, esbuild, and TypeScript), upstream patch and minor updates frequently introduce subtle behavioral changes or breakages. Pinning ensures that what users install has been fully verified against our test suites. If an application needs an immediate patch before a CLI release, package manager overrides (npm or pnpm) or resolutions (yarn) can be used in the workspace `package.json`.

2. **Automated security scanning:** We already use automated tooling Renovate across the repository that tracks security advisories and opens PRs for dependency updates. While updates on LTS branches are handled more conservatively to maintain stability, we prioritize critical security updates whenever necessary.

3. **Release cadence**: We ship regular releases every Wednesday. If a critical zero-day vulnerability directly impacts the production runtime, we issue an immediate out-of-band release. However, for build-time tooling where high-severity CVEs often turn out to be false alarms or unexplainable in CLI usage we follow our regular weekly schedule to ensure thorough testing and validation before releasing

It might be a partial solution though to check which dependencies stick to SemVer fairly closely and replace their pinned version by a "~x.y.z" style constraint. I mean expecting every maintainer of an Angular dependent project to override the pinned version constraint in one of Angular's packages on their own risk just to see the same change being made by the Angular maintainers about a week or so later does not seem like a proper way to handle this.
